summary: This program stores three Java collection terms and their definitions in a Map, looks one definition up by its term, and then lists every term in alphabetical order.

lines.text: Map is the interface that describes a collection of key-value pairs; the variable below is declared with this type so the code depends on the general idea of a map rather than one specific implementation.
HashMap is the concrete class that actually stores the pairs, using hashing for fast lookup.
TreeSet keeps its elements permanently sorted, which is how the alphabetical listing at the end is produced without writing any sorting code.
The two type parameters say that both keys and values are text: the key is the term, the value is its definition. The empty angle brackets on the right let Java infer the same types again.

lines.code: glossary.put("List", "An ordered collection (also known as a sequence) that may contain duplicate elements. Allows positional access and insertion of elements.");
lines.text: put stores a definition under a term. Calling put again with the same key would replace the old definition instead of adding a second entry, because map keys are unique.
Holding the search term in a variable means the lookup and the printed label can never disagree.
get returns the value stored under a key, or null if the key was never added, so a lookup is a single fast operation rather than a scan through the whole collection.
The \n escape sequence starts a new line before the heading, leaving a blank line that separates the two sections of output.

keySet gives a view of just the terms, and passing it to the TreeSet constructor copies them into a set that orders strings alphabetically. A HashMap gives no guarantee about the order of its keys, so this step is what makes the output predictable.
The enhanced for loop visits each element in turn, and because the source is a TreeSet those elements arrive already in order.
